newsitem.title: FRANCE: Iraq crisis impact on wheat prices seen limited.
newsitem.headline: Iraq crisis impact on wheat prices seen limited.

text.p: The renewed hostilities in Iraq that suspended its oil-for-food agreement with the U.N. will depress declining world wheat prices, European grain traders said, but the impact would be limited.

"This is not good for the market," one trader said on Tuesday, hours after the United States launched missile attacks on Iraqi targets. "But I expect only limited pressure on already easier world prices," he said.
World wheat prices have slipped in recent weeks as good harvests in many regions have increased supply.
Another trader said the crisis has boosted oil prices because the oil side of the exchange deal had been concluded and Iraqi oil was on the verge of being shipped into world markets.

But discussions on food and humanitarian supplies - notably wheat and flour - which were due to be sent to Iraq were at an early stage, and contracts which might have influenced market prices had not been struck.
"So far it has been talk, talk, and no action," one trader said.
"There were already a lot of arguments over how the U.N. would perform and safeguard the operation," another trader said.

The U.S. missile attack on Iraqi defence targets was launched in retaliation for Iraq's incursions into its Kurdish northern province -- a move that prompted the U.N. on Sunday to delay the oil-for-food exchange agreed in May.

Under the terms of that deal, Iraq would be allowed to sell $2 billion worth of crude over six months to buy food and medicine for its people suffering from U.N. sanctions imposed after Iraq invaded Kuwait in 1990.
Iraq began studying purchases of wheat and flour on grain markets in the summer but was awaiting final U.N. purchase rules to conclude the deals.
One trader said Iraq was expected to buy up to one million tonnes of wheat, with an initial tender for 200,000 tonnes expected soon.

Another trader said Iraq was in talks to import flour, with France, Turkey and India tipped as likely suppliers. France has traditionally been a major food supplier to Iraq, and a French banker said millers were keen on resuming business with Iraq.

Traders generally took news of Tuesday's missile attack in their stride, saying the exchanges would eventually come through. One trader said they would probably be implemented after the U.S. presidential election in November.
